text: Ten years after filming a group of Swedish teenagers, Stefan Jarl went back to see what the decade had done. The people are the same — Kenta, Stoffe, the others from Dom kallar oss mods — but the terms have changed: a girlfriend, a small son, a mother to visit at Kronoberg, heroin arriving in the middle of everything. Sequels are a fiction habit. A documentary that waits a decade is doing something else, closer to keeping an appointment than continuing a story, and the ten years show in faces rather than being announced. Jarl films it plainly, letting a prison visit or a phone call carry the weight that argument would flatten. Sweden entered it for the Academy Awards, the Guldbagge for Best Film went to it, and it appears on FLM's list of the best Swedish films. What it records is ordinary time doing its work on people once photographed as a movement.

A London insurance office mutinies, hoists a sail, and puts to sea as a pirate ship. That is roughly the register Terry Jones works in for 107 minutes, built as vignettes rather than a plot: hospital staff arriving to collect a liver while the donor is still using it, an eater pursuing appetite past the point where a joke normally stops. Anthologies are fragile things. The audience has to reinvest every few minutes, and one flat segment drags on everything around it, so the strategy here is to push each piece as far as it will go and let the joins show. The announced subject is taken at face value and answered in the register of a cheap pamphlet, which is the gag and also the position. Cannes gave it the Grand Prix, a sentence that sits oddly next to a film this committed to bad taste.

The fire goes out, and nobody in the tribe knows how to make another. Three men go looking for more, on a route nobody has mapped, with the understanding that what they carry back cannot be improvised if it dies on the way. Jean-Jacques Annaud spends the hundred minutes on procedure, on how a flame is fed and sheltered and guarded through a night, and lets the tension come from the arithmetic of fuel. The Academy gave the film its award for makeup, which sounds peripheral and is closer to the center: the whole argument runs through bodies, postures, brow ridges, a face registering an idea it has no word for. Then there is Ika, who already knows what the warriors were sent to find, and the balance of the journey shifts.

A war film in which the soldier at its center cannot get up, cannot answer, and has one shell's worth of history behind him. Dalton Trumbo builds the whole picture from what a man in that condition still holds: the years before the artillery found him, arriving out of sequence, in whatever shape memory gives them. The formal problem is severe. A protagonist who cannot act turns every scene into either a recollection or a room where nothing outside can change, and the film accepts both constraints rather than cheating around them with battlefield spectacle. The stake is not survival, which the premise has already settled. It is whether anything of a person continues when the equipment for expressing it is gone. Cannes gave it the Grand Prix in 1971, half a century after the war it describes.

A murder file lands on the desk of a newly promoted captain, and the promotion turns out to be the smaller event. Dominik Moll keeps his police work in Grenoble and lets the routine run at its real speed: interviews, timelines, one more name out of Clara's life, then another, each producing more biography and less answer. The patience is deliberate to the point of discomfort. What the film is actually watching is not the case but the squad, the effect on men of returning daily to one killing they are expected to explain, and the way method starts to look like a coping device. It took the César for Best Film. The unease it leaves comes from something admitted quietly underneath the procedure: the tools these officers were trained on may not fit what is being asked of them.

An industrialist sits through a Racine tragedy to watch his niece in a bit part, and comes out rearranged by something he did not go for. Agnès Jaoui builds the film on that mismatch and refuses to let it travel in the obvious direction. Castella is blunt, practical and uninterested in art until he is not, and the cultivated people around him are not thereby right about anything. The comedy lives in watching taste behave like a class marker everyone insists is a personal quality, with each judgment made in one room overheard in the next. The record: a César for supporting actress, the European Film Award for Best Film, France's place in the Academy's international category. What holds it together is the sound of people talking past one another while certain they are being perfectly clear.

In occupied Paris a man buys pictures cheap from people who need to leave the country quickly, and does not consider this a crime. Then his name turns up attached to somebody else. Joseph Losey sets it in 1942 and makes the machinery of the period entirely clerical: what closes on Robert Klein is not a soldier but a file, a card index, an administrative resemblance between two men who share a name. Everything runs on the assumption that a mistake can be corrected by the same offices that produced it, and the assumption gets expensive. Losey takes 123 minutes and stays cold, leaving the dealer's own conduct standing in plain view rather than pleading it away. The César for Best Film went to it. What it examines is how thin the difference is between a man and his paperwork.

Berlin has been made one city on paper, and that is where the trouble begins. Wim Wenders takes 147 minutes at an odd altitude: angels who hear everything and touch nothing, moving through a place that got what it asked for and now carries crime, money and a heavy American presence along with it. The premise sounds weightless. In practice it enforces a specific kind of attention, since to a listener with all the time there is, nobody in the frame is background and no conversation is filler. Unification is treated not as an event but as an aftermath, something the city was still digesting in 1993. Cannes gave it the Grand Prix. The longing runs in both directions, angels toward flesh and the city toward whatever it was before, and that double pull is what the length is for.

The problem is standing water on a poor lord's land. The remedy, it turns out, is a talent for saying cruel things quickly. Patrice Leconte constructs a court comedy in which wit is not ornament but the only working currency: at Versailles an engineering proposal cannot be argued through, it can only be charmed through, and a man who cannot hold a room will never get his ditches dug. The rules are strict and the film obeys them, which keeps it from becoming a parade of costume, though the costumes did take a César. A hesitation carries the consequence a lost battle carries elsewhere. 102 minutes, lean for a period piece, and France sent it to the Academy Awards. The arithmetic is what stays: every epigram in it has somebody's drainage riding on the outcome.

At eight, a boy has worked out what the household expects him to be, and obliges. Guillaume Gallienne turns that arrangement into 85 minutes of comedy, and the choice of register is the whole gamble: told straight, the material is a case study of a family deciding a child's nature before the child can object; told fast, it becomes something an audience can laugh at without losing sight of the cost. The mother is the fixed point. Everything the film knows about performance it learns from a household where one person's certainty organizes everyone else. It took the César for Best Film alongside the César for Best First Film, an unusual pairing, plus the Valois d'or. Autobiography played as comedy, at speed, is a peculiar act of nerve.

A man who has spent his working life in a shipyard on the southern French coast decides, late, that he will feed people instead. Venice gave the film its Grand Jury Prize and it took the Louis Delluc, but the shape is what registers: 155 minutes for an ambition that modest, and the length is the method rather than an excess. Abdellatif Kechiche lets scenes run to the size they would run to in life, so the film accumulates instead of advancing, and the daughter of his partner does more of the pushing than he does. The stakes are small and total at once. A middle-aged laborer with one idea left, in a country where his family is old news to itself and a question to everybody else, is betting on the only thing he still has time to build.

Two men, one instrument, and an unsettled disagreement about what music is for. Alain Corneau begins with a widower who has withdrawn from the world and kept only his playing, then introduces the one thing capable of disturbing such a person: a young man who wants to be taught. The film declines to make the older musician sympathetic. His refusal of company is presented as a position rather than a symptom, and the lessons run closer to interrogation than to encouragement. Césars went to the lead performance, the cinematography and the costumes, which indicates where the weight sits: on faces, cloth and sound rather than on anything spoken. 115 minutes and almost no incident, and the question stays open, playing to be heard or playing because the silence is otherwise unendurable.

Ink is a trade before it is a vocation, and this poet grew up around machines that print other men's words. Lucien de Rubempré leaves the family press for Paris believing that talent is what the city buys. Xavier Giannoli spends 149 minutes laying out the actual market: how a reputation gets manufactured, what a favorable word costs, who collects on it. Period costume is not the subject. The subject is a commercial apparatus for converting opinion into money, set out with enough procedural detail that the machinery keeps looking familiar, and against it a provincial with a good ear and no protection. It won the César for Best Film. What the film is finally about is pricing: how a young man's estimate of himself gets revised downward, transaction by transaction.

The antagonist is a records office, and it has no idea it is in a comedy. Albert Dupontel runs 87 minutes on a collision between three people with urgent private business and the counters, forms and waiting rooms standing between any of them and their own past: a hairdresser out of time, a man whose career has quit on him, an archivist who cannot see the archive. The pacing is farce. The ground underneath it is not. Suze's search exists only because something done to a fifteen-year-old was written down somewhere and then buried by process, which makes every joke about paperwork a claim about who is permitted to retrieve a life. It took the César for Best Film, the prize voted by high school students, and the Goya for best European film. Short, fast, and unwilling to let the laugh cancel the grief.
